newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK windfall tax can safely take 5 bln stg.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK windfall tax can safely take 5 bln stg.

text.p: The British government is expected to raise five billion sterling with a proposed windfall tax in its budget next week, but any attempt to raise more is seen provoking a legal backlash, a Reuters survey showed.
The median of 19 forecasts for the amount expected to be raised with a windfall tax was five billion sterling, in the survey of 20 economists carried out between June 19 and 20.
Ten contributors to the survey gave a figure for how much money could be raised without risking a legal challenge. The median of these predictions was five billion sterling.

"Five billion is about the upper limit of what they can achieve without a legal challenge. The bigger it is the more likely it is to be challenged," said David Smith, chief economist at Williams de Broe.

In their pre-election manifesto, Britain's new Labour government outlined plans to collect a one-off tax on profits of Britain's privatised utility companies to fund a welfare-to-work programme for the unemployed.
The independent Institute of Fiscal Studies has called the windfall tax an arbitrary measure that was difficult to reconcile with any principles of equitable taxation.
As yet, the government has not said what criteria it would use to determine eligibility for the tax or how the windfall will be applied.
Estimates of how much the government may try to raise via this tax ranged from three to seven billion sterling.
"It's difficult to second guess this sort of thing. They might try and collect three billion sterling for three years," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse.
Predictions of how much could be raised without risking a legal challenge ranged from zero to 10 billion sterling.

Water and electricity companies are seen as the most likely candidates for the one-off tax. Some contributors also expect privatised rail operators, British Telecom, airport operator BAA, British Airways and gas company BG plc to be affected.
Only one contributor saw the tax being levied on British Steel and one expected the windfall to be applied to the privatised coal industries.
